# static-website pack

The release standard for a plain static site: the date-anchored version scheme, release-on-push, the explicit publish set, the GitHub Pages deploy, and the PR gate — the contract and its setup in [the **static-site-releases** skill](skills/static-site-releases/SKILL.md), the **vendored pipeline** in [`stubs/`](stubs/) (materialized into each site repo's own `.github/`), the eight in-session rules in [RULES.md](RULES.md), and the conformance checks beside them. **Opt-in**: a project declares it in `.claudinite-settings.json` when it's ready to ship a site this way. GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow / composite action from a repo's own `.github/`, so the pack holds the templates and each repo hosts a managed copy — no cross-repo `@main` dependency, and the repo's own values live in one `.github/site.config`.

Fingerprint: the `Release static site` orchestrator (`.github/workflows/static-site-release.yml` carrying that `name:`). It only *suspects* the pack — declaring is the project's call. Every rule here is gated on it too, so a repo that declares the pack for the versioning and CI half while its site deploys somewhere other than GitHub Pages carries none of the deploy machinery and none of these rules fire on it.

## Checks

| Check | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sw/release-workflows` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `sw/site-config` | high | correctness | check: blocking |
| `sw/version-scheme` | medium | correctness | check: blocking |
| `sw/version-bumped` | high | correctness | check: blocking |

What each holds:

- `sw/release-workflows` — the orchestrator (named, push-triggered, calling the local publish reusable), both reusable workflows, all three composite actions, and a PR gate are vendored.
- `sw/site-config` — `.github/site.config` exists with its five explicit keys, no unknown keys, every publish path tracked, no tooling directory published, and an `index.html` in the set.
- `sw/version-scheme` — every declared version record carries the same `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` version.
- `sw/version-bumped` — a change that touches the publish set raises the version in the same change. Work-scope: the tree always carries a version, and only the diff says whether it moved with the published files beside it.

## Skills

[**static-site-releases**](skills/static-site-releases/SKILL.md) is the standard itself — the
version scheme, the publish set, `.github/site.config`, the vendored workflows and actions, the
setup a new site repo needs, and the one-time GitHub settings no automation can turn on. It is the
contract the four checks above judge against, reached when a pipeline is being set up or debugged
rather than carried by every session in the repo. The rule that the pipeline files are managed
copies of the pack's stubs lives there too, forced for the `static-site-*` workflows it concerns.

## Rules (`RULES.md`)

| Rule | Severity | Reason | Enforcement |
|---|---|---|---|
| The publish set names every published file | high | correctness | prose: <200 words + check (`sw/site-config`) |
| The version moves with the change | high | correctness | prose: <200 words + checks (`sw/version-bumped`, `sw/version-scheme`) |
| The site is served from a subpath | high | correctness | prose: <100 words |
| Freshness is a published manifest's job | high | correctness | prose: <200 words |
| Nothing attests to its own freshness | high | correctness | prose: <200 words |
| Split caches join across generations | critical | correctness | prose: <200 words |
| Follow missing data to the pixel | high | correctness | prose: <200 words |

The version scheme and the code that computes it live together in [stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs](stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs) — the checks import `VERSION_RE` from there rather than restating it, so the rule and the bump can't disagree about what a version is.
=========== RULES ===========
# Static website

- **A published file is a file the publish set names — adding a page is two edits.** The Pages
  artifact is assembled from `.github/site.config`'s `publish_paths` and nothing else, so a new
  page, stylesheet or data file that isn't under a published path (or named in the list) is simply
  absent from the live site, with no error anywhere: the build is green, the deploy succeeds, the
  page 404s. When you add a file the site serves, put it under an already-published directory or add
  it to `publish_paths` in the same change. The list is additive on purpose — the alternative,
  "publish the repo minus what we remember to exclude", publishes every draft, note and key nobody
  thought to hide.

- **The version moves with the change.** A change touching the published site raises
  `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` in the same PR —
  `node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs $(version_files)` computes it from the previous
  version and the UTC date, and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds the line. Never hand-write the
  `ymmdd` or the counter: a typed value either collides with a released one or is dated in the
  future, and the next bump refuses. The release flow writes no version of its own — it ships what
  it finds on `main` — so a shipped change without a bump is never released at all. The one
  deliberate human part is the **major**, a "this is a new generation of the site" statement; the
  owner's **"bump version"** means exactly that, and the release workflow's `bump: major` dispatch
  is what performs it.

- **The site is served from a subpath, not a domain root.** GitHub Pages serves it at
  `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/` (unless a custom domain is configured), so a root-relative URL
  — `/style.css`, `/img/logo.png`, a `fetch('/data.json')` — resolves above the site and 404s in
  production while working fine in a local `file://` or `python -m http.server` preview. Write
  links, asset paths and fetches **relative** to the page.

- **Freshness is a published manifest's job, not a per-file TTL's.** There is no server here to vary
  `Cache-Control` per file, so the freshness policy moves into the client — and the shape it
  reaches for first, giving each file a lifetime matching how fast you think it changes, reprices
  the same bet on every file and gets it wrong in both directions at once: too long and visitors
  read stale data, too short and they re-download what never changed. Publish one small manifest
  naming every downloadable asset and a hash of its contents, fetch *that* on each load, and evict
  exactly the entries whose hash moved. It buys longer caching **and** fresher data, which no TTL
  can offer together, and the extra request is the one you are probably already making for a version
  string. Expect a mismatch mid-deploy — the manifest is fetched, a deploy lands, the asset that
  follows disagrees — so refetch once and carry on; only a disagreement that survives fresh copies
  of both is a fault worth surfacing.

- **Nothing can attest to its own freshness, and size attests to nothing at all.** A stale file
  carries a perfectly valid hash *of itself*, and an internal `"version"` field states which
  generation it is, never whether that generation is still current — so the expected hash has to
  come from a file fetched fresher than the one being judged, which is what makes the manifest the
  one asset that may never carry a TTL of its own. Caching it saves no round-trip; it moves the
  staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor is length a cheap stand-in for a hash: a correction
  applied uniformly across a file is routinely byte-length-neutral — a timezone fix rewriting
  every `16:25` to `17:25` moved **0 bytes** of a 3.1 MB catalogue while changing the meaning of
  every record in it. And record the manifest's hash beside the entry as you write it, so the check
  is a string compare; re-hashing the stored body means pushing megabytes through a digest on the
  critical path of every load to answer a question the bookkeeping already knows.

- **Two files cached on separate clocks and later joined *will* be joined across generations —
  make them a verified set or don't split them.** Splitting a payload so each half caches on its own
  schedule is a sound instinct and it has this cost: every visitor eventually holds one half from
  Tuesday and the other from Thursday. Content-addressed keys ("name the row by its date and time,
  not its position in the array") survive rows being *added and removed*, which is what they are
  usually chosen for, and not a systematic *correction to the key itself* — a timezone shift, a
  rounding change, a rename — which moves every key at once and joins the two halves to nothing.
  Have each half record the generation of the other and refetch both on a mismatch. Then assert on
  the join *rate*, because a partial join is silent by construction: a missing key returns "no data
  for this row", which is indistinguishable from a row that genuinely has none yet, and a check
  written as "at least one row joined" passes at 6%.

- **Don't call missing data survivable until you have followed it to the pixel.** "The fetch is
  allowed to fail — it'll just show as unknown, which we already handle" is a claim about every
  consumer downstream, and it is usually wrong: an absent value reaching a boolean, a comparison or
  a status lookup is very often indistinguishable from a real negative, so the page renders a
  confident falsehood with nothing logged and the visitor acts on it. Trace the missing value all
  the way to what it draws before deciding a failure is tolerable. Where it isn't, the file is
  required — fail the load and show the error state, because a wrong answer with no error is worse
  than an error.

  — `/style.css`, `/img/logo.png`, a `fetch('/data.json')` — resolves above the site and 404s in
  production while working fine in a local `file://` or `python -m http.server` preview. Write
  links, asset paths and fetches **relative** to the page.

- **Freshness is a published manifest's job, not a per-file TTL's.** There is no server here to vary
  `Cache-Control` per file, so the freshness policy moves into the client — and the shape it
  reaches for first, giving each file a lifetime matching how fast you think it changes, reprices
  the same bet on every file and gets it wrong in both directions at once: too long and visitors
  read stale data, too short and they re-download what never changed. Publish one small manifest
  naming every downloadable asset and a hash of its contents, fetch *that* on each load, and evict
  exactly the entries whose hash moved. It buys longer caching **and** fresher data, which no TTL
  can offer together, and the extra request is the one you are probably already making for a version
  string. Expect a mismatch mid-deploy — the manifest is fetched, a deploy lands, the asset that
  follows disagrees — so refetch once and carry on; only a disagreement that survives fresh copies
  of both is a fault worth surfacing.

- **Nothing can attest to its own freshness, and size attests to nothing at all.** A stale file
  carries a perfectly valid hash *of itself*, and an internal `"version"` field states which
  generation it is, never whether that generation is still current — so the expected hash has to
  come from a file fetched fresher than the one being judged, which is what makes the manifest the
  one asset that may never carry a TTL of its own. Caching it saves no round-trip; it moves the
  staleness up a level and hides it better. Nor is length a cheap stand-in for a hash: a correction
  applied uniformly across a file is routinely byte-length-neutral — a timezone fix rewriting
  every `16:25` to `17:25` moved **0 bytes** of a 3.1 MB catalogue while changing the meaning of
  every record in it. And record the manifest's hash beside the entry as you write it, so the check
  is a string compare; re-hashing the stored body means pushing megabytes through a digest on the
  critical path of every load to answer a question the bookkeeping already knows.

- **Two files cached on separate clocks and later joined *will* be joined across generations —
  make them a verified set or don't split them.** Splitting a payload so each half caches on its own
  schedule is a sound instinct and it has this cost: every visitor eventually holds one half from
  Tuesday and the other from Thursday. Content-addressed keys ("name the row by its date and time,
  not its position in the array") survive rows being *added and removed*, which is what they are
  usually chosen for, and not a systematic *correction to the key itself* — a timezone shift, a
  rounding change, a rename — which moves every key at once and joins the two halves to nothing.
  Have each half record the generation of the other and refetch both on a mismatch. Then assert on
  the join *rate*, because a partial join is silent by construction: a missing key returns "no data
  for this row", which is indistinguishable from a row that genuinely has none yet, and a check
  written as "at least one row joined" passes at 6%.

- **Don't call missing data survivable until you have followed it to the pixel.** "The fetch is
  allowed to fail — it'll just show as unknown, which we already handle" is a claim about every
  consumer downstream, and it is usually wrong: an absent value reaching a boolean, a comparison or
  a status lookup is very often indistinguishable from a real negative, so the page renders a
  confident falsehood with nothing logged and the visitor acts on it. Trace the missing value all
  the way to what it draws before deciding a failure is tolerable. Where it isn't, the file is
  required — fail the load and show the error state, because a wrong answer with no error is worse
  than an error.

# Releasing a static site

Every static-site repo of ours ships the **same** pipeline: same workflows, same versioning, same
publish-set rules, same CI gate — so set a new repo up against that contract rather than authoring its
pipeline, and turn on by hand only the GitHub settings the automation cannot.

The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this pack's [`stubs/`](../../stubs/) — the
[orchestrator](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml), three `workflow_call`-only **reusable
workflows** ([publish](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-publish.yml),
[deploy](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml),
[bump](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-bump-version.yml)), the
[CI gate](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml), and three composite actions
([read-site-config](../../stubs/actions/read-site-config/action.yml),
[bump-site-version](../../stubs/actions/bump-site-version/action.yml),
[assemble-site](../../stubs/actions/assemble-site/action.yml)) — and **vendored into each site repo's own
`.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no cross-repo dependency. GitHub resolves a
reusable workflow or a composite action only from a repo's own `.github/`, never from the shared
mount, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo hosts a
*managed* copy: edit the pack, not the copy. Everything repo-specific is the keys of
`.github/site.config`, so every vendored file is copy-verbatim across repos.

## The contract

### Versioning — `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>`

The site's version is **date-anchored**, and it is computed, never typed. The scheme, and the code
that computes it, live together in [bump.mjs](../../stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs):

| Part | What it is |
|---|---|
| `major` | the wrap counter. Raised by hand only as a deliberate "new generation of the site" statement — and automatically on the decade wrap (below). |
| `ymmdd` | the **last digit of the UTC year**, then `MM`, then `DD`. 2026-12-31 → `61231`; 2027-01-01 → `70101`. |
| `n` | the day's release counter: `1` for the day's first release, the previous release's `n + 1` for each further release the **same** day. |

**Why the year digit.** The bare `MMDD` form is not monotonic across a year boundary: December
31st's `1.1231.3` sorts *above* the next day's `1.0101.1`, so "later" stopped meaning "bigger" —
which is the one thing every reader of a version assumes. Prefixing the year digit restores it:
`1.61231.3` → `1.70101.1`.

**The decade wrap.** One year digit means 2029-12-31 (`91231`) is followed by 2030-01-01 (`00101`)
— the one legitimate decrease. The major absorbs it: `1.91231.4` → `2.00101.1`, and the ordering
holds forever. Any *other* decrease (a version dated in the future — a hand edit, a wrong clock) is
an error and fails the bump loudly; burning a major to paper over it would hide a real problem.

**The bump belongs to the change, not to the pipeline.** A change that touches the publish set
raises the version in the same PR — `node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs $(the repo's
version_files)` writes every record together — and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds that line. The
release flow writes no version at all: it releases whatever it finds on `main`, and no-ops when that
version already has a release. So the number a reviewer sees on a PR is the number that ships, and a
published change that forgot its bump fails on the PR rather than silently never deploying. A change
that publishes nothing needs no bump and redeploys nothing.

**The major is the one bump the pipeline still performs**, because it belongs to no single change:
dispatch **Release static site** with `bump: major` and it raises the major, pushes it, and releases
the result. That dispatch is what **"bump version"** means on a site repo.

**Moving an existing site onto the scheme** is a one-line edit, once: rewrite the current version
in place with the year digit inserted (`1.1231.3` → `1.61231.3`). The result is strictly greater
than what it replaces (`61231 > 1231`), so no tag or release ordering is disturbed and no major
bump is needed. Every version after that is the next change's bump.

The version lives in the files the repo names in `version_files` — the first is the source of
truth, the rest must agree. `sw/version-scheme` holds them to the scheme and to each other; the
bump validates every record before writing any, so a failure never leaves a half-bumped tree.

The rejected alternative is subtractive — "serve the repo except `.claude/` and `.claudinite/`" —
and it fails in the direction that hurts: it publishes every file nobody thought to exclude, and it
publishes each *new* one silently, the day it lands. An additive list can only publish what the

publishes each *new* one silently, the day it lands. An additive list can only publish what the
repo asked for, and its failure mode (a file that doesn't appear) is visible on the site and caught
on the PR. Two guards make that concrete, in [assemble-site](../../stubs/actions/assemble-site/action.yml):
a publish path that doesn't exist fails the run, and so does an assembled site with no `index.html`
at its root. Both also run on every pull request, so a broken publish set never reaches `main`.

### `.github/site.config` — five required keys, no defaults

A dotenv file, **every required key explicit**. A default that "happens to match" a repo's
layout silently publishes the wrong tree the day the layout or the default changes:

| Key | What it is |
|---|---|
| `publish_root` | the directory the site is rooted at; `.` = the repo root. It becomes the site's `/`. |
| `publish_paths` | the publish set: space-separated files/directories under `publish_root`. |
| `version_files` | space-separated version records; the first is the source of truth. |
| `build_command` | what produces the publish set; `""` = nothing to build, stated. |
| `test_command` | the repo's gate; `""` = no tests, stated. |

A command that needs dependencies installs them itself (`npm ci && npm test`) — that's why there is
no "setup" key and no assumption that a lockfile exists.

#### `build_vars` — the one optional key

`build_command` otherwise runs with no access to any repo configuration at all, which leaves a site
needing a build-time value (an analytics token, a base URL, a feature flag) with nowhere to put it.
`build_vars` is the declaration that closes that gap: space-separated names of **repo variables**,
exported into the build's environment before `build_command` runs.

```dotenv
build_command=node tools/build.mjs
build_vars=SITE_ANALYTICS_TOKEN SITE_BASE_URL
```

Three properties are load-bearing, and each is the opposite of a nearby easier choice:

- **Optional, unlike the five.** The explicitness rule exists to stop a default from publishing the
  *wrong tree*; an absent `build_vars` can't do that — it means the build sees no variables, exactly
  what every site did before the key existed. So an untouched config keeps its exact meaning and no
  existing repo has to be migrated to stay valid.
- **A declared-but-unset variable fails the run.** Exporting an empty string instead would give the
  original failure one level down: the build succeeds, the page ships, and the feature that needed
  the value is silently dead on the live site. Better a failed deploy naming the variable.
- **Variables, never secrets.** The exporter is handed `toJSON(vars)`, a context that structurally
  cannot carry a secret — so a value that must not appear in a published artifact cannot reach the
  step that produces one. That boundary is a property of what the workflow passes, not a convention
  to remember. A build that genuinely needs a secret is doing something a published static site
  should not be doing.

Declaring `build_vars` also holds the repo to a vendored copy new enough to honour it: `sw/release-workflows`
fails if the config names variables while the vendored action or workflows predate the exporter, since
that combination reads the key, ignores it, and builds with the variables unset.

```dotenv
# A hand-authored site with no build step.
publish_root=.
publish_paths=index.html about.html assets data
version_files=package.json
build_command=
test_command=npm ci && npm test
```

`read-site-config` fails the run on a missing file, a missing or empty required key, or an unknown
(typo'd) key; `sw/site-config` fails the same cases in the repo's own checks, plus a publish path
that matches nothing tracked, a tooling directory in the publish set, and a site with no
`index.html`.

### The workflows

**One orchestrator per repo** — [`static-site-release.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml),
named exactly `Release static site`. It owns only the triggers (push to `main`, plus a
`workflow_dispatch` with `force`) and calls the local publish reusable, which runs:

| Stage | What it does |
|---|---|
| `check` | is a release due? The version on `main` has no release of its own yet — or `force`. Asking the **release list** for the current version (rather than diffing files against a tag) is what makes the flow idempotent: a failed run retries on the next push with nothing to undo, and a push carrying an already-released version is a clean no-op. |
| `verify` | the repo's `test_command`, on the tree being released — **before** anything is tagged or deployed. |
| `release` | GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at that tree, auto-generated notes. |
| `deploy` | the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish set. |
| `report-failure` | any failure above opens a fresh `workflow-failure` issue and closes earlier open ones for this workflow as duplicates, so the newest failure is the single open bug to triage. |

The `bump: major` dispatch pushes with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which fires no workflow — which is why the
orchestrator runs the release explicitly after it rather than relying on the push trigger, and why
the push cannot loop.

A push carrying a version that is already released is a clean no-op: no tag, no redeploy.

**CI** — [`static-site-ci.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml) runs on every pull request with
**no `paths:` filter**: the Claudinite world sweep, the repo's `test_command`, the build, and a dry
run of the artifact assembly. The missing path filter is deliberate — a path-filtered conformance
flow arms auto-merge and then never runs, so the repo's own maintenance PR waits forever.

## Setting up a new site repo

1. **Declare** `static-website` in `.claudinite-settings.json` and answer the pack's two adoption
   questions (where it's served; what's published). Re-vendor so the pack's tree lands under the
   shared mount.
2. **Vendor the pipeline** into the repo's own `.github/`: everything under
   [`stubs/workflows/`](../../stubs/workflows/) and [`stubs/actions/`](../../stubs/actions/). There are no
   tokens to replace. A repo whose site deploys somewhere **other** than Pages takes the CI stub
   and the versioning half only, and skips the orchestrator + the three reusables — every rule in
   this pack is gated on the orchestrator, so nothing here fires on it.
3. **Write `.github/site.config`** with all five required keys, from the adoption answers (plus
   `build_vars` if the build needs repo variables).
4. **Put the version on the scheme** — one hand edit in each `version_files` record (`1.1231.3` →
   `1.61231.3` for an existing site; `1.<today's ymmdd>.1` for a new one).
5. **Open the one-time settings issue** (below) — idempotent: search the tracker first and skip if
   one already exists, open or closed.
6. Run the world sweep; `sw/release-workflows`, `sw/site-config` and `sw/version-scheme` are the
   checklist for whether the wiring is complete. `sw/version-bumped` is work-scope and shows up on
   the first PR that touches the publish set.

## The settings only a human can turn on

Repository settings are not repo content: no workflow, check or agent can set them, and a pipeline
that silently depends on one is a pipeline that fails on its first run for a reason nobody wrote
down. So they are tracked as **state, in one issue in the adopting repo** — done once, then closed
— not as a standing file:

```markdown

  step that produces one. That boundary is a property of what the workflow passes, not a convention
  to remember. A build that genuinely needs a secret is doing something a published static site
  should not be doing.

fails if the config names variables while the vendored action or workflows predate the exporter, since
that combination reads the key, ignores it, and builds with the variables unset.

```dotenv

publish_root=.
publish_paths=index.html about.html assets data
version_files=package.json
build_command=
test_command=npm ci && npm test
```

`read-site-config` fails the run on a missing file, a missing or empty required key, or an unknown
(typo'd) key; `sw/site-config` fails the same cases in the repo's own checks, plus a publish path
that matches nothing tracked, a tooling directory in the publish set, and a site with no
`index.html`.

### The workflows

**One orchestrator per repo** — [`static-site-release.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml),
named exactly `Release static site`. It owns only the triggers (push to `main`, plus a
`workflow_dispatch` with `force`) and calls the local publish reusable, which runs:

| Stage | What it does |
|---|---|
| `check` | is a release due? The version on `main` has no release of its own yet — or `force`. Asking the **release list** for the current version (rather than diffing files against a tag) is what makes the flow idempotent: a failed run retries on the next push with nothing to undo, and a push carrying an already-released version is a clean no-op. |
| `verify` | the repo's `test_command`, on the tree being released — **before** anything is tagged or deployed. |
| `release` | GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at that tree, auto-generated notes. |
| `deploy` | the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish set. |
| `report-failure` | any failure above opens a fresh `workflow-failure` issue and closes earlier open ones for this workflow as duplicates, so the newest failure is the single open bug to triage. |

The `bump: major` dispatch pushes with `GITHUB_TOKEN`, which fires no workflow — which is why the
orchestrator runs the release explicitly after it rather than relying on the push trigger, and why
the push cannot loop.

A push carrying a version that is already released is a clean no-op: no tag, no redeploy.

**CI** — [`static-site-ci.yml`](../../stubs/workflows/static-site-ci.yml) runs on every pull request with
**no `paths:` filter**: the Claudinite world sweep, the repo's `test_command`, the build, and a dry
run of the artifact assembly. The missing path filter is deliberate — a path-filtered conformance
flow arms auto-merge and then never runs, so the repo's own maintenance PR waits forever.

4. **Put the version on the scheme** — one hand edit in each `version_files` record (`1.1231.3` →

There's no `stateless-website` pack on the shelf — I'll assume you mean **`static-website`** (the neighbours with similar names are `cloudflare-site` and `host-page`).

## What it is

[`packs/static-website/`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs/static-website) is **the release standard for a plain static site**. Not a site-building pack — a shipping pack. It is opt-in (declared by hand), fingerprinted by `.github/workflows/static-site-release.yml` carrying the name `Release static site`, and it lists `html` as its companion pack.

Its central claim: every static-site repo of ours ships the *same* pipeline, so you set a repo up against a contract rather than authoring its pipeline.

## The four things it carries

**1. A vendored CI/release pipeline** ([`stubs/`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs/static-website/stubs)) — five workflows and three composite actions. One orchestrator (`Release static site`, push-to-`main` + dispatch), three `workflow_call`-only reusables (publish, deploy-to-Pages, bump-version), a CI gate with deliberately no `paths:` filter, and the actions `read-site-config`, `bump-site-version`, `assemble-site`. The pack holds the templates; each site repo hosts a *managed copy* in its own `.github/`, because GitHub resolves reusables and composite actions only from a repo's own `.github/`, never from the shared mount. A [standing migration record](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/migrations/2026-07-31-static-site-vendoring/migration.mjs) re-materializes that set every converge cycle, so a canon fix reaches all site repos overnight and a hand-edited copy self-heals.

**2. A date-anchored version scheme** — `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>`, computed by [`bump.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs), never typed. `ymmdd` is the last digit of the UTC year plus `MMDD` (the year digit exists because bare `MMDD` isn't monotonic across New Year); the decade wrap is the one legitimate decrease and the major absorbs it. The bump belongs to the *change*, not the pipeline — the release flow ships whatever version it finds on `main` and no-ops if that version already has a release. The major is the one bump the pipeline still performs, and that dispatch is exactly what the owner's **"bump version"** means on a site repo.

**3. `.github/site.config`** — a dotenv with five *required, no-default* keys (`publish_root`, `publish_paths`, `version_files`, `build_command`, `test_command`) plus one optional `build_vars` (repo variables exported into the build; structurally cannot carry secrets). The publish set is additive on purpose: the subtractive alternative publishes every draft and key nobody remembered to exclude.

**4. Seven in-session rules** ([`RULES.md`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/RULES.md)) — and these are the interesting half, because they're not about CI at all. Three are pipeline discipline (publish set names every file; the version moves with the change; the site is served from a *subpath*, so root-relative URLs 404 in production while working locally). Four are hard-won client-side caching lessons for a world with no server to set `Cache-Control`: freshness is a published manifest's job, not a per-file TTL's; nothing can attest to its own freshness and size attests to nothing (the cited case: a timezone fix rewrote every record of a 3.1 MB catalogue and moved **0 bytes**); two files cached on separate clocks *will* be joined across generations, so assert the join *rate* — "at least one row joined" passes at 6%; and don't call missing data survivable until you've followed it to the pixel.

## Enforcement

| Check | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `sw/release-workflows` | the orchestrator, both reusables, all three actions and a PR gate are vendored — and fails if `build_vars` is declared against a copy too old to honour it |
| `sw/site-config` | the five keys present, no unknown keys, every publish path tracked, no tooling dir published, an `index.html` in the set |
| `sw/version-scheme` | every `version_files` record on the scheme and agreeing |
| `sw/version-bumped` | work-scope: a diff touching the publish set raises the version in the same change |

All four blocking. The checks import `VERSION_RE` from `bump.mjs` rather than restating it, so the rule and the bump can't disagree.

Plus the [`static-site-releases`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/skills/static-site-releases/SKILL.md) skill, which is the contract itself — force-loaded on edits to `.github/site.config` and `.github/workflows/static-site-*.yml`, and carrying the new-repo setup plus the one-time GitHub settings no automation can turn on (tracked as a single issue in the adopting repo, not a standing file).

The design's through-line: every rule in the pack is gated on the orchestrator, so a repo that adopts it for the versioning and CI half while deploying somewhere other than Pages takes the CI stub only and none of these rules fire on it.

Checked the gating in code rather than trusting the README's summary — the answer is narrower than the README implies, and one claim in it is wrong.

## What survives without the Pages half

**1. The seven prose rules — all of them, unconditionally.** Prose is injected per *declared* pack ([`generate-rules-index.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/engine/pack_loader/generate-rules-index.mjs)); `detect` is a fingerprint suggestion, not a prose gate. So every session in the repo carries all seven. Four of them — manifest-not-TTL, nothing attests to its own freshness, split caches join across generations, follow missing data to the pixel — are about a **client fetching files with no server to set `Cache-Control`**, which is true on Cloudflare, S3 or any bucket. That's the pack's most transferable content and it has nothing to do with Pages. "Publish set names every file" and "the version moves with the change" still apply if you keep `site.config`. Only "served from a subpath" is genuinely Pages-shaped, and it becomes noise on a repo with a domain root.

**2. `sw/version-scheme` — the one check that still fires.** It gates on `.github/site.config` existing, not on the orchestrator. So the `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` scheme and record-agreement stay enforced.

**3. The versioning mechanics themselves** — [`bump.mjs`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/stubs/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs) plus the skill's reasoning behind it (the year digit for cross-New-Year monotonicity, the decade wrap absorbed by the major, computed-never-typed). Entirely host-agnostic.

**4. `.github/site.config` as a declared contract** — five explicit keys, no defaults, plus `build_vars`. Useful on its own as "what's published / what builds it / what gates it", read by `read-site-config`.

**5. The CI stub** — world sweep, `test_command`, build, dry-run assembly. Only the last step leans Pages-ward, and it really just asks "does the publish set assemble".

**6. `requires: ['html']`**, so declaring it pulls the markup pack in.

## What you lose — including things you'd expect to keep

Three of the four checks are gated on `shipsPipeline` and go silent:

- `sw/release-workflows` — and the check that the **CI stub is vendored at all** lives *inside* that gate (`release-workflows.mjs:122`). So the half you kept has no conformance check.
- `sw/site-config` — the five-keys / paths-tracked / no-tooling-dir / `index.html` enforcement is gone, even though `sw/version-scheme` still reads that same file.
- `sw/version-bumped` — "the version moves with the change" keeps its prose and loses its teeth, which is the point of the versioning half.
- The [standing migration record](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/migrations/2026-07-31-static-site-vendoring/migration.mjs) is gated on the orchestrator's `name:` too, so your CI stub and two actions are a **one-time copy that drifts forever** — no self-heal, no canon fixes.

**All in all:** prose worth having on any host, a version scheme, a config vocabulary, and one CI file — with the enforcement of the retained half deleted along with the half you dropped.

## One thing that looks like a defect

[`pack.mjs:11-13`](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/pack.mjs) and the README both state "every rule here is relevance-gated on it, so nothing fires on that repo." `sw/version-scheme` isn't — it gates on `site.config`. Two sibling checks over the same file with two different gates, and the prose isn't gated at all, so "none of these rules fire on it" is wrong twice over.

Answering only — nothing filed or edited, per your dismissal.

## What survives when you drop the Pages half

The skill's own step 2 says such a repo "takes the CI stub and the versioning half only, and skips the orchestrator + the three reusables." Concretely, four things:

**1. `.github/site.config`** — the five required, no-default keys (`publish_root`, `publish_paths`, `version_files`, `build_command`, `test_command`) plus optional `build_vars`. Entirely host-agnostic. The reasoning is too: an additive publish set can only publish what the repo asked for, and `build_vars` carries repo *variables* not secrets, because the exporter is handed `toJSON(vars)` — a context that structurally cannot hold one.

**2. The version scheme and `bump.mjs`** — `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>`, computed never typed, monotonic across the New Year, decade wrap absorbed by the major, a future-dated version failing loudly. It's a plain node script run inside a change; it never touches Pages.

**3. The CI workflow** (`static-site-ci.yml`) — and this keeps more of the pipeline than "skip the deploy half" suggests. It still uses `read-site-config`, `export-build-vars` and `assemble-site`, so all three composite actions stay vendored. It runs the world sweep, the repo's `test_command`, the build with declared variables exported, and a dry-run assembly. Plus the deliberate no-`paths:`-filter decision, which is really a Claudinite-maintenance fact, not a Pages one: a path-filtered conformance flow arms auto-merge and then never runs.

**4. The four caching rules** — and these are the part with no connection to Pages, to GitHub, or to releases at all. Manifest-over-per-file-TTL; nothing can attest to its own freshness and byte-length attests to nothing (the timezone fix that moved 0 bytes of a 3.1 MB catalogue); two files cached on separate clocks will be joined across generations, so assert the join *rate*; and don't call missing data survivable until you've followed it to the pixel. That's the durable half of the pack for any static site anywhere.

## What you lose — more than the docs claim

Release-on-push, the idempotent "is a release due?" check against the release list, the tag and GitHub Release, the Pages deploy, and `report-failure`'s issue-opening. Also the `bump: major` dispatch, which means **"bump version" has no implementation on such a repo** — the one deliberately human part of the scheme loses its mechanism.

Two sharper losses the README doesn't surface:

- **The vendored copies stop self-healing.** The standing [migration record](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/main/packs/static-website/migrations/2026-07-31-static-site-vendoring/migration.mjs) gates on `.github/workflows/static-site-release.yml` — the orchestrator. A non-Pages repo's CI stub and three actions are re-materialized by nothing, so a canon fix never reaches them and a hand-edit never heals. "Edit the pack, not the copy" stops being true exactly there.
- **Three of the four checks go silent.** `sw/release-workflows`, `sw/site-config` and `sw/version-bumped` all open with `if (!shipsPipeline(ctx)) return []`. So the publish-set correctness check and "the version moves with the change" both stop holding — on the very repo that kept the versioning half and still needs them.

## One thing the pack says about itself that isn't so

`pack.mjs` says "every rule here is relevance-gated on it, so nothing fires on that repo," and the README repeats it. Two parts of that don't hold:

- `sw/version-scheme` gates on `.github/site.config` existing, not on the orchestrator — it never imports `shipsPipeline`. It fires.
- The seven prose rules aren't gated at all. `generate-rules-index.mjs` builds the index from `declaredPacks`; `detect` is a fingerprint, not a prose gate. All seven load into every session in any declaring repo.

The skill also force-loads on `.github/workflows/static-site-*.yml`, which the surviving CI stub matches. And `requires: ['html']` pulls the html pack in regardless.

So the real answer: without Pages you get a versioning convention, a publish-set declaration, one CI workflow, and a solid body of client-side caching doctrine — but you keep exactly one of four checks, lose the self-healing, and the pack's own description of that configuration is wrong in a way that would mislead someone deciding whether to adopt it.

> ⚠️ Still open: the `pack.mjs`/README claim that nothing fires on a non-Pages repo is inaccurate (`sw/version-scheme` + all prose). You dismissed the question on what to do about it — nothing filed, nothing edited.

########## stubs/workflows/static-site-release.yml
name: Release static site

# THE ORCHESTRATOR of the static-website release standard — the one entry point
# every static-site repo of ours carries, vendored from the pack into this repo's
# own .github/ (GitHub resolves a reusable workflow or composite action only from
# the repo's own .github/, never from a mount). It owns the TRIGGERS and nothing
# else: the logic lives in the local reusable workflows it calls, and every
# repo-specific value comes from this repo's `.github/site.config` (read inside
# those workflows), so this file is copy-verbatim in every site repo.
#
# Release on push: any push to main whose version has not been released yet cuts
# a release — tag it, deploy the site. The version comes from the CHANGE, not
# from here: a PR touching the published site raises it in the same PR
# (`sw/version-bumped`), so an ordinary README or tooling commit carries the
# version that is already out and is a clean no-op.
#
# The dispatch form has two knobs, and they compose:
#   * bump: major  — the deliberate "new generation of the site" statement, the
#                    one version write this pipeline still performs. It pushes
#                    the bump to main and then releases it.
#   * force: true  — release even when the version on main is already released
#                    (a rebuild after a settings fix, a first deploy on a repo
#                    whose site predates the pipeline). Redeploys the existing
#                    tag rather than cutting a second one.
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      bump:
        description: "Raise the version before releasing"
        type: choice
        options: [none, major]
        default: none
      force:
        description: "Release even when the version on main is already released"
        type: boolean
        default: false

# One release at a time, and never cancel one mid-flight: a cancelled run can
# leave the version bumped with no release or deploy behind it.
concurrency:
  group: static-site-release
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  # Dispatch-only, and only when asked for. The push trigger never reaches it,
  # so nothing writes a version unattended.
  bump:
    if: inputs.bump == 'major'
    permissions:
      contents: write
    uses: ./.github/workflows/static-site-bump-version.yml

  release:
    needs: bump
    # `always()` so the skipped bump job (every push, and every dispatch that
    # asked for no bump) does not skip the release with it; the explicit result
    # test still stops a failed bump from releasing a half-written version.
    if: always() && needs.bump.result != 'failure' && needs.bump.result != 'cancelled'
    permissions:
      contents: write   # create the release
      pages: write      # deploy the site
      id-token: write   # the OIDC token deploy-pages exchanges
      issues: write     # the failure reporter
    uses: ./.github/workflows/static-site-publish.yml
    with:
      force: ${{ inputs.force || false }}

# THIS PIPELINE WRITES NO VERSION. The version belongs to the change that
# earned it: a PR touching the published site raises it in the same PR (the
# pack's `sw/version-bumped` check holds that line), so what reaches main is
# already the number to release. A deliberate generation bump — the major — is
# the orchestrator's `bump` dispatch, which pushes a bump and lets the ordinary
# push trigger release it.
#
# The pipeline, in order — and the order is the point: nothing is tagged or
# deployed until the tests that guard the site have passed.
#
#   check    is a release due? The version on main has no release of its own
#            yet — or `force`. Asking the RELEASE for the current version
#            (rather than diffing files against a tag) is what makes the flow
#            idempotent: a day whose run failed retries on the next push with
#            nothing to undo, and a push that only touched tooling carries the
#            same version and is a clean no-op.
#   verify   the repo's own gate (`test_command`), on the tree being released.
#   release  GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at that tree, with
#            auto-generated notes.
#   deploy   the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish
#            set.
#
# The caller must grant `permissions: contents: write, pages: write,
# id-token: write, issues: write`.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      force:
        description: "Release even when the version on main is already released"
        required: false
        type: boolean
        default: false

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    outputs:
      release: ${{ steps.due.outputs.release }}
      version: ${{ steps.due.outputs.version }}
      released: ${{ steps.due.outputs.released }}
      test_command: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.test_command }}
      sha: ${{ steps.head.outputs.sha }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          # The branch tip as of now, not github.sha (the tip when the push
          # landed) — anything merged in between rides along in this release.
          ref: main
          # Full history + tags: the tag test below reads them.
          fetch-depth: 0

      # Pin that tip once, here: every later stage checks out THIS sha, so the
      # tree that is tested is the tree that is tagged and deployed.
      - id: head
        run: echo "sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

      - id: cfg
        uses: ./.github/actions/read-site-config

      - name: Has the version on main been released yet?
        id: due
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          FORCE: ${{ inputs.force }}
          # Intentionally word-split below into the individual version records.
          VERSION_FILES: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.version_files }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          # The bump script is also the version READER, so nothing else has to
          # know how a repo's version record is shaped.
          version="$(node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs --print $VERSION_FILES)"
          echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          released=false
          if gh release view "v$version" >/dev/null 2>&1 || git rev-parse "v$version" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
            released=true
          fi
          echo "released=$released" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          if [ "$released" = "false" ]; then
            echo "v$version is not released yet — releasing." | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
            echo "release=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          elif [ "$FORCE" = "true" ]; then
            echo "v$version is already released — forced, so redeploying it without a new tag." | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
            echo "release=true" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          else
            echo "v$version is already released — nothing to do. Raise the version in the change that needs releasing." | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
            echo "release=false" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          fi

  # purpose: a failed gate must leave the tag and the live site exactly as they
  # were.
  verify:
    needs: check
    if: needs.check.outputs.release == 'true' && needs.check.outputs.test_command != ''
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}
      # No install step and no npm cache: a test_command that needs dependencies
      # says so itself (`npm ci && npm test`), which keeps the config to the five
      # keys and never assumes a lockfile a plain HTML repo doesn't have.
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - name: Run the repo's gate
        run: ${{ needs.check.outputs.test_command }}

  release:
    needs: [check, verify]
    # `always()` so the skipped verify job (a repo that states test_command="")
    # does not skip the release with it; the explicit result test still stops a
    # real failure. A forced redeploy of an already-released version has nothing
    # to cut, so the job runs only for a version with no release of its own.
    if: >-
      always() && needs.check.outputs.release == 'true' &&
      needs.check.outputs.released == 'false' &&
      needs.verify.result != 'failure' && needs.verify.result != 'cancelled'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}
          fetch-depth: 0
      - name: Cut the GitHub Release
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          VERSION: ${{ needs.check.outputs.version }}
          SHA: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          gh release create "v$VERSION" --target "$SHA" --title "v$VERSION" --generate-notes
          echo "Released v$VERSION." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

  # The site itself, from the exact commit that was released.
  deploy:
    needs: [check, release]
    if: >-
      always() && needs.check.outputs.release == 'true' &&
      needs.release.result != 'failure' && needs.release.result != 'cancelled'
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pages: write
      id-token: write
    uses: ./.github/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml
    with:
      ref: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}

  # Release-on-push is unattended once the merge is done — a red run in the
  # Actions list reaches nobody. Converge any failure in this pipeline (its own
  # jobs and the called deploy alike) to a fresh tracking issue, superseding the
  # earlier open ones for this workflow so the newest failure is always the
  # single open bug to triage.
  report-failure:
    needs: [check, verify, release, deploy]
    if: failure()
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      issues: write
    steps:
      - name: Open a fresh failure issue and dedup earlier ones
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
          RUN_URL: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}
          RUN_ID: ${{ github.run_id }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          prefix="⚠️ Workflow failing: Static site: Publish"
          title="${prefix} — $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d) (run ${RUN_ID})"
          # GitHub never creates a label on demand, and listing by a missing
          # label errors — so create it idempotently first.
          gh label create workflow-failure --repo "$REPO" --color B60205 \
            --description "An unattended workflow failed and needs a human" 2>/dev/null || true
          mapfile -t olds < <(gh issue list --repo "$REPO" --label workflow-failure \
            --state open --json number,title --limit 100 \
            -q "map(select(.title | startswith(\"$prefix\"))) | .[].number")
          url="$(gh issue create --repo "$REPO" --title "$title" --label workflow-failure \
            --body "The static-site release pipeline failed: [view run](${RUN_URL}). The site was NOT redeployed. Close this once the cause is fixed.")"
          new="${url##*/}"
          for n in "${olds[@]:-}"; do
            [ -n "$n" ] || continue
            gh issue comment "$n" --repo "$REPO" --body "Duplicate of #${new} — superseded by the latest failure of this workflow."
            gh issue close "$n" --repo "$REPO" --reason "not planned" 2>/dev/null || gh issue close "$n" --repo "$REPO"
          done

########## stubs/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml
name: "Static site: Deploy to GitHub Pages (reusable)"

# Deploys the repo's EXPLICIT publish set to GitHub Pages. Vendored from the
# static-website pack into the repo's own .github/; workflow_call ONLY — it is
# invoked by "Static site: Publish" at the released commit, so what is live is
# always exactly what was tagged. A repo never dispatches it directly.
#
# The artifact is assembled by the assemble-site composite action from
# `publish_root` + `publish_paths` — an additive list, so the agent-tooling dirs
# (.claude/, .claudinite/), dev tooling, notes and anything else unlisted are
# absent by construction rather than by remembering to exclude them. That also
# sidesteps the dangling-symlink trap that breaks a whole-root Pages upload:
# upload-pages-artifact tars with --dereference, and .claude/skills/* are
# symlinks into the gitignored corpus, empty on a runner.
#
# One-time owner setup in the calling repo: Settings → Pages → Source =
# "GitHub Actions". Until that is set, deploy-pages fails; the caller's failure
# reporter opens the tracking issue.
#
# The calling job must grant `permissions: contents: read, pages: write,
# id-token: write`.
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Commit to deploy (empty = the default checkout)"
        required: false
        type: string
        default: ""

# Least privilege for a Pages deploy: read the repo, write Pages, mint the OIDC
# token deploy-pages exchanges.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never run two Pages deploys at once; let an in-flight deploy finish.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          ref: ${{ inputs.ref }}

      - id: cfg
        uses: ./.github/actions/read-site-config

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.build_command != ''
        with:
          node-version: 22

      # Repo variables the config declares, exported into the build's env.
      # `vars` structurally cannot carry a secret, which is the point: this
      # feeds the step that produces the published artifact.
      - name: Export the declared build variables
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.build_vars != ''
        env:
          DECLARED_BUILD_VARS: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.build_vars }}
          REPO_VARS_JSON: ${{ toJSON(vars) }}
        run: node .github/actions/read-site-config/export-build-vars.mjs

      # A build_command that needs dependencies installs them itself
      # (`npm ci && npm run build`) — see the config's keys.
      - name: Build the site
        if: steps.cfg.outputs.build_command != ''
        run: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.build_command }}

      - uses: ./.github/actions/assemble-site
        with:
          publish_root: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.publish_root }}
          publish_paths: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.publish_paths }}

      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v5

      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: _site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4
########## stubs/workflows/static-site-bump-version.yml
name: "Static site: Bump version (reusable)"

# The DELIBERATE version bump, vendored from the static-website pack into the
# repo's own .github/. workflow_call ONLY — the `static-site-release.yml`
# orchestrator owns the trigger.
#
# This is the pipeline's ONLY write to a version, and it is never automatic. The
# routine bump belongs to the change that earned it: a PR touching the published
# site raises the version in the same PR, and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds
# that line. What is left over is the generation statement — "this is a new site"
# — which belongs to no single change, so a human dispatches it here.
#
# The date-anchored scheme has no minor: `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` computes its last
# two parts, so the major is the only part anyone chooses. Raising it restarts
# the day counter at today.
#
# The bump is pushed to main with GITHUB_TOKEN, which fires no workflow — hence
# the orchestrator running the release explicitly after this rather than relying
# on the push trigger.
#
# The caller must grant `permissions: contents: write`.
on:
  workflow_call:
    outputs:
      version:
        description: The version after the bump
        value: ${{ jobs.bump.outputs.version }}

defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash

jobs:
  bump:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.bump.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          # The branch tip as of now. If main moves before the push below it
          # fails non-fast-forward — a loud red, and nothing has been released
          # off a half-written version.
          ref: main

      - id: cfg
        uses: ./.github/actions/read-site-config

      - id: bump
        uses: ./.github/actions/bump-site-version

name: "Static site: Deploy to GitHub Pages (reusable)"

# Deploys the repo's EXPLICIT publish set to GitHub Pages. Vendored from the
# static-website pack into the repo's own .github/; workflow_call ONLY — it is
# invoked by "Static site: Publish" at the released commit, so what is live is
# always exactly what was tagged. A repo never dispatches it directly.
#
# The artifact is assembled by the assemble-site composite action from
# `publish_root` + `publish_paths` — an additive list, so the agent-tooling dirs
# (.claude/, .claudinite/), dev tooling, notes and anything else unlisted are
# absent by construction rather than by remembering to exclude them. That also
# sidesteps the dangling-symlink trap that breaks a whole-root Pages upload:
# upload-pages-artifact tars with --dereference, and .claude/skills/* are
# symlinks into the gitignored corpus, empty on a runner.
#
# One-time owner setup in the calling repo: Settings → Pages → Source =
# "GitHub Actions". Until that is set, deploy-pages fails; the caller's failure
# reporter opens the tracking issue.
#
# The calling job must grant `permissions: contents: read, pages: write,
# id-token: write`.

  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      ref:
        description: "Commit to deploy (empty = the default checkout)"
        required: false
        type: string
        default: ""

# Least privilege for a Pages deploy: read the repo, write Pages, mint the OIDC
# token deploy-pages exchanges.
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write

# Never run two Pages deploys at once; let an in-flight deploy finish.
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false

    shell: bash

# The DELIBERATE version bump, vendored from the static-website pack into the
# repo's own .github/. workflow_call ONLY — the `static-site-release.yml`
# orchestrator owns the trigger.
#
# This is the pipeline's ONLY write to a version, and it is never automatic. The
# routine bump belongs to the change that earned it: a PR touching the published
# site raises the version in the same PR, and `sw/version-bumped` is what holds
# that line. What is left over is the generation statement — "this is a new site"
# — which belongs to no single change, so a human dispatches it here.
#
# The date-anchored scheme has no minor: `<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` computes its last
# two parts, so the major is the only part anyone chooses. Raising it restarts
# the day counter at today.

# the orchestrator running the release explicitly after this rather than relying
# on the push trigger.
#
# The caller must grant `permissions: contents: write`.

        value: ${{ jobs.bump.outputs.version }}

### One-time GitHub settings for the static-site release pipeline

The release pipeline is vendored and green in CI, but the following are repository *settings* —

# Website release flows — alignment design

> **Status: not implemented.** Proposed, owner review pending — a design under discussion, not a
> description of how the release flows work today.

Status: **proposed** (owner review pending). Refs #722.
Inputs: [COMPARISON.md](COMPARISON.md) (the fleet evidence), [SOUNDNESS.md](SOUNDNESS.md)
(the independent soundness analysis). The subject is the `static-website` pack — merged in
#611 — and the three site repos' bespoke flows it is meant to replace.

> **State note (2026-08-09, evening).** After this design was written, canon merged #729
> (`build_vars`) and EdFringeNow adopted the pack (#319) — see the state updates in
> COMPARISON.md and SOUNDNESS.md. Per the owner's instruction, that movement is treated
> as *data, not as the desired outcome*: this design's conclusions stand where they
> disagree with what shipped. Decisions affected by the new state say so inline.

## Goal

One github-pages-serving standard, owned by the pack, with:

- **no bespoke release mechanism left in any site repo** — the bespoke deploy workflows,
  bump scripts and CI variants all go;
- **minimum GitHub Actions surface** — YAML only where the platform forces it (triggers,
  permissions, OIDC, the Pages actions); all logic in scripts the ordinary vendoring
  converges. The rule of thumb the owner stated holds: a step that needs a secret or the
  repo token must run in Actions; nothing else has to;
- **minimum manual repo settings** — a fresh repo that declares the pack releases on the
  first push, with the custom domain as the only genuinely manual item;
- **customization without forks** — everything repo-specific in `.github/site.config`;
  the workflows stay copy-verbatim.

The acceptance probe (owner-specified): purge every release-related aspect *and setting*
from MissingBulbWebsite so it simulates a new repo, adopt the pack, and the first release
must work on the first go.

## Decisions

### D1. Keep one pack; reshape `static-website` in place

The consolidation policy survives the soundness review intact — one vendored standard,
repo-specifics in a small explicit config. The pack is reworked in place; with EdFringeNow
now adopted (#319), the reshape carries one live adopter's vendored copies along — a
normal converge plus one agent-stage handoff for its workflow files, small and bounded,
rather than the zero-cost rework the original draft assumed. The pack keeps its
`static-website` id (it owns
versioning and CI, not just serving); renaming to `github-pages-serving` is possible but
buys nothing the id doesn't already say — owner's call, recorded as an open question.

What survives unchanged from #611: the `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` scheme (it fixes the bespoke
`mmdd` year-boundary flaw), the 5-key `site.config` with no defaults, the additive publish
set with its two loud guards, release-due-by-tag, the ordered check → verify → bump →
Release → deploy stages, and the adoption interview (which is what forces EdFringeNow's
root-publish conversation).

### D2. Thin-shim shape: two entry-point workflows, logic in the mount

SOUNDNESS.md finding 4: only *entry-point/reusable workflows* are location-bound to
`.github/workflows/`; composite actions and scripts are not, and the current 4-workflow +
3-action vendored surface (~890 lines per repo) maximizes exactly the file class the
converge machinery is worst at (GITHUB_TOKEN cannot push workflow files — every pack

+# The logic behind every static-site repo's release, vendored from the
+# static-website pack into the repo's own .github/. workflow_call ONLY — the
+# `static-site-release.yml` orchestrator owns the triggers and passes no repo
+# values; everything repo-specific comes from `.github/site.config` via the
+# read-site-config composite action.
+# THIS PIPELINE WRITES NO VERSION. The version belongs to the change that
+# earned it: a PR touching the published site raises it in the same PR (the
+# pack's `sw/version-bumped` check holds that line), so what reaches main is
+# already the number to release. A deliberate generation bump — the major — is
+# the orchestrator's `bump` dispatch, which pushes a bump and lets the ordinary
+# push trigger release it.
+# The pipeline, in order — and the order is the point: nothing is tagged or
+# deployed until the tests that guard the site have passed.
+#   check    is a release due? The version on main has no release of its own
+#            yet — or `force`. Asking the RELEASE for the current version
+#            (rather than diffing files against a tag) is what makes the flow
+#            idempotent: a day whose run failed retries on the next push with
+#            nothing to undo, and a push that only touched tooling carries the
+#            same version and is a clean no-op.
+#   verify   the repo's own gate (`test_command`), on the tree being released.
+#   release  GitHub Release `v<major>.<ymmdd>.<n>` at that tree, with
+#            auto-generated notes.
+#   deploy   the Pages deploy of that exact commit, from the explicit publish
+#            set.
+# The caller must grant `permissions: contents: write, pages: write,
+# id-token: write, issues: write`.
+on:
+  workflow_call:
+    inputs:
+      force:
+        description: "Release even when the version on main is already released"
+        required: false
+        type: boolean
+        default: false
+defaults:
+  run:
+    shell: bash
+jobs:
+  check:
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    permissions:
+      contents: read
+    outputs:
+      release: ${{ steps.due.outputs.release }}
+      version: ${{ steps.due.outputs.version }}
+      released: ${{ steps.due.outputs.released }}
+      test_command: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.test_command }}
+      sha: ${{ steps.head.outputs.sha }}
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
+        with:
+          # The branch tip as of now, not github.sha (the tip when the push
+          # landed) — anything merged in between rides along in this release.
+          ref: main
+          # Full history + tags: the tag test below reads them.
+          fetch-depth: 0
+      # Pin that tip once, here: every later stage checks out THIS sha, so the
+      # tree that is tested is the tree that is tagged and deployed.
+      - id: head
+        run: echo "sha=$(git rev-parse HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+      - id: cfg
+        uses: ./.github/actions/read-site-config
+      - name: Has the version on main been released yet?
+        id: due
+        env:
+          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
+          FORCE: ${{ inputs.force }}
+          # Intentionally word-split below into the individual version records.
+          VERSION_FILES: ${{ steps.cfg.outputs.version_files }}
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          # The bump script is also the version READER, so nothing else has to
+          # know how a repo's version record is shaped.
+          version="$(node .github/actions/bump-site-version/bump.mjs --print $VERSION_FILES)"
+          echo "version=$version" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
+          released=false
+          if gh release view "v$version" >/dev/null 2>&1 || git rev-parse "v$version" >/dev/null 2>&1; then
+            released=true
+          fi
+          echo "released=$released" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

+            echo "v$version is not released yet — releasing." | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

+          else
+            echo "v$version is already released — nothing to do. Raise the version in the change that needs releasing." | tee -a "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

+      contents: read
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
+        with:
+          ref: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}

+      # says so itself (`npm ci && npm test`), which keeps the config to the five
+      # keys and never assumes a lockfile a plain HTML repo doesn't have.
+      - uses: actions/setup-node@v5

+      - name: Run the repo's gate
+        run: ${{ needs.check.outputs.test_command }}

+    needs: [check, verify]

+    # does not skip the release with it; the explicit result test still stops a
+    # real failure. A forced redeploy of an already-released version has nothing
+    # to cut, so the job runs only for a version with no release of its own.
+      always() && needs.check.outputs.release == 'true' &&
+      needs.check.outputs.released == 'false' &&

+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    permissions:
+      contents: write
+    steps:
+      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
+        with:
+          ref: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}
+          fetch-depth: 0

+        env:
+          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
+          VERSION: ${{ needs.check.outputs.version }}
+          SHA: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          gh release create "v$VERSION" --target "$SHA" --title "v$VERSION" --generate-notes
+          echo "Released v$VERSION." >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
+  # The site itself, from the exact commit that was released.
+  deploy:
+    needs: [check, release]
+      always() && needs.check.outputs.release == 'true' &&
+      needs.release.result != 'failure' && needs.release.result != 'cancelled'

+      contents: read
+      pages: write
+      id-token: write
+    uses: ./.github/workflows/static-site-deploy-pages.yml
+    with:
+      ref: ${{ needs.check.outputs.sha }}
+  # Release-on-push is unattended once the merge is done — a red run in the
+  # Actions list reaches nobody. Converge any failure in this pipeline (its own
+  # jobs and the called deploy alike) to a fresh tracking issue, superseding the
+  # earlier open ones for this workflow so the newest failure is always the
+  # single open bug to triage.
+  report-failure:
+    needs: [check, verify, release, deploy]
+    if: failure()
+    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    permissions:
+      issues: write
+    steps:
+      - name: Open a fresh failure issue and dedup earlier ones
+        env:
+          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
+          REPO: ${{ github.repository }}
+          RUN_URL: ${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}
+          RUN_ID: ${{ github.run_id }}
+        run: |
+          set -euo pipefail
+          prefix="⚠️ Workflow failing: Static site: Publish"
+          title="${prefix} — $(date -u +%Y-%m-%d) (run ${RUN_ID})"
+          # GitHub never creates a label on demand, and listing by a missing
+          # label errors — so create it idempotently first.
+          gh label create workflow-failure --repo "$REPO" --color B60205 \
+            --description "An unattended workflow failed and needs a human" 2>/dev/null || true
+          mapfile -t olds < <(gh issue list --repo "$REPO" --label workflow-failure \
+            --state open --json number,title --limit 100 \
+            -q "map(select(.title | startswith(\"$prefix\"))) | .[].number")
+          url="$(gh issue create --repo "$REPO" --title "$title" --label workflow-failure \
+            --body "The static-site release pipeline failed: [view run](${RUN_URL}). The site was NOT redeployed. Close this once the cause is fixed.")"
+          for n in "${olds[@]:-}"; do
+            [ -n "$n" ] || continue
+            gh issue comment "$n" --repo "$REPO" --body "Duplicate of #${new} — superseded by the latest failure of this workflow."
+            gh issue close "$n" --repo "$REPO" --reason "not planned" 2>/dev/null || gh issue close "$n" --repo "$REPO"
+          done
